title: Peopling of the Americas
summary: The ancestors of Indigenous Americans came from northeast Asia by way of Beringia and spread to the tip of South America. Footprints in New Mexico suggest people were south of the ice sheets by about 23,000 years ago, a date still debated.
card: Genomes show that Indigenous Americans descend from a population that split from East Asians roughly 26,000–24,000 years ago and paused, probably near Beringia, before spreading south. How early that spread began is argued: White Sands footprints point to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, while sceptics see the main expansion only after 16,000 years ago. The Clovis-first model is gone, the coastal and inland routes are both still in play, and even the long-accepted Monte Verde site in Chile was challenged in 2026.
what:
The peopling of the Americas is the process by which humans first reached North and South America and spread through them. Genetic studies indicate that Indigenous Americans descend from one ancestral population that separated from East Asians about 26,100–23,900 years ago and then lived in isolation long enough for distinctive founder lineages to form, a pause called the Beringian standstill. Tamm and colleagues (2007) placed that isolation in Beringia, the land exposed between Siberia and Alaska when sea level was low; others note it could have been anywhere from the Lake Baikal region to Hokkaido. After the pause, people spread quickly: the founder lineages are spread evenly from north to south rather than nested.

For decades many archaeologists held that the makers of Clovis tools, now dated to 13,050–12,750 calibrated years before present (cal BP), were the first Americans. That model was abandoned as older sites were accepted and genomes showed earlier occupation. The infant Anzick-1, buried with Clovis tools in Montana about 12,700–12,550 cal BP, belonged to a population closely related to all Indigenous Americans and directly ancestral to many.

The starting date is contested. Human footprints at White Sands National Park, New Mexico, made by many teenagers and children on the shores of Ice Age Lake Otero, are bracketed by radiocarbon dates on seeds of the aquatic plant Ruppia cirrhosa of about 22,900–21,100 cal BP, inside the Last Glacial Maximum. Critics argued that the seeds could have absorbed old carbon and might be thousands of years too old; a 2023 study dated land-plant pollen from the same layers and got matching ages. Other specialists still put the main expansion after about 16,000 years ago, with the earliest securely dated sites after about 15,000. Monte Verde in southern Chile, dated to about 14,500 cal BP and long the strongest pre-Clovis site, was argued in 2026 to be mid-Holocene in age, a reading its excavators and other geoarchaeologists reject. Whether the first migrants used the Pacific coast, open by about 17,000 years ago, or an inland ice-free corridor is unresolved, and some Indigenous nations hold origin accounts that reject a migration from Asia.

uncertainty.note: Years converted from calibrated radiocarbon years before present (BP = before 1950) as year = 1950 − cal BP. Start = c. 23,000 cal BP, the earliest bracket of the White Sands footprints (Bennett et al. 2021: Ruppia seed ages 22.86 ± 0.32 to 21.13 ± 0.25 ka, N = 11; Pigati et al. 2023 pollen and OSL ages agree). start_plus_years 8000 covers the critics' alternative of c. 15,000–13,000 cal BP (Oviatt et al. 2022) and the view that expansion began only after ~16,000 years ago (Potter et al. 2018). End = c. 12,750 cal BP, the close of Clovis, by which time Clovis and Fishtail complexes span both continents; this end point is an editorial convention, not a recorded event. Pre-LGM claims older than 23 ka are not adopted here.

how: The process turned on ice and sea level. (1) During the last glaciation, sea level fell far enough to expose Beringia, a broad land connection between Siberia and Alaska; plant remains about 18,000 years old preserved in ash from a Devil Mountain eruption in Alaska match its last proposed opening. (2) In the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000–19,000 years ago, the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets coalesced, closing both the interior ice-free corridor and, in southeastern Alaska, the Pacific coast, where the ice margin peaked about 20,000–17,000 years ago. (3) Cut off, the ancestral population stood still: mitochondrial founder lineages A2, B2, C1, D1 and others accumulated mutations that separate them from their Asian sister lineages, and the Ancient Beringian branch split off about 22,000–18,000 years ago. (4) As ice retreated, the coast opened first: by about 17,000 years ago southeastern Alaska offered an open path with productive marine and land ecosystems. The interior corridor opened physically between about 15,600 and 14,800 years ago and became biologically viable by 13,000–12,600 years ago in one reading, or as early as 15,000–14,000 in another. (5) Once south of the ice, people spread rapidly: founder lineages appear across both continents, northern and southern branches split about 17,500–14,600 years ago, and Clovis in North America and Fishtail points in South America are continent-wide by 13,000–12,900 cal BP. If the White Sands dates are right, some people were already south of the ice before the LGM closed the routes, so the first crossing must predate the closure.
why_it_matters: This process produced the founding ancestry of Indigenous peoples across the Americas (later pulses of gene flow from Asia added to it among some northern groups) and set the stage for all later human history in the hemisphere: independent plant domestication, the Classic Maya, Tenochtitlan and Cusco all grew from populations whose roots lie in this dispersal. It also matters for how science works. The Clovis-first model, built on a narrow window of 13,050–12,750 cal BP, dominated for decades and was overturned by sites and genomes, and the same contest continues over White Sands and, since 2026, over Monte Verde. The dates decide basic questions. If the White Sands footprints are 23,000–21,000 years old, people were south of the ice before the Last Glacial Maximum closed both the coastal and interior routes, so the coast-versus-corridor debate would concern later movements rather than the first arrival; had the footprints instead been 15,000–13,000 years old, as critics proposed, they would fit the older consensus of expansion after 16,000 years ago. At White Sands, people and megafauna shared the lakeshore for at least two millennia, which bears on whether people drove late Pleistocene extinctions. Finally, the research touches living communities. The Anzick-1 genome was studied after consultation with several tribal nations, many of whose representatives asked for reburial, and Indigenous scholars and elders have argued that framing their ancestors simply as migrants can be used to weaken ties to land.

related.because: The dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa and across Asia produced the northeast Asian population from which the ancestors of Native Americans separated about 26,000–24,000 years ago.

related.title: Last Glacial Maximum
related.because: Lowered sea level during the glaciation exposed the Beringian land bridge, while coalesced ice sheets closed the routes south and are thought to have isolated the founding population in the Beringian standstill.
By settling both continents, the first Americans established the populations whose descendants later developed farming independently in the Americas, without contact with the Old World centres.

perspectives.holder: Bennett, Bustos, Pigati, Springer and colleagues (Science 2021, 2022 reply, 2023); USGS and NPS
perspectives.account: Footprints at White Sands Locality 2 are bracketed by seed ages of about 23,000–21,000 cal BP, and terrestrial pollen and luminescence dates from the same layers agree, so people were south of the ice sheets during the Last Glacial Maximum.

perspectives.holder: Madsen et al. (Science comment, 2022); Oviatt, Madsen, Rhode and Davis (Quaternary Research, 2022)
perspectives.account: Ruppia is an aquatic plant that takes up old dissolved carbon; living Ruppia collected in 1947 gave an apparent age of about 7,400 years, so the footprints could be roughly 15,000–13,000 years old. They called for pollen and luminescence dating, which the 2023 study then supplied.

Genetic and archaeological data put ancestral Native American expansion after about 16,000 years ago, with the earliest securely dated sites after about 15,000; both a coastal and an interior route remain viable and neither can yet be rejected.

The ice-free corridor was not biologically viable until about 13,000 or 12,600 years ago, too late for the first migrants; the southeastern Alaska coast was open and productive after about 17,000 years ago and is the more likely early route.

perspectives.holder: Clovis-first model (dominant for decades; now abandoned, as described by Waters et al. 2020 and Rasmussen et al. 2014)
perspectives.account: The makers of Clovis tools were the first people in the Americas. Sites older than Clovis, Western Stemmed points as old as or older than Clovis, a Fishtail complex established in South America by about 12,900 cal BP, and genetic evidence for earlier occupation have overturned this view.

perspectives.holder: Dillehay and colleagues (PLOS ONE 2015; Science eLetter 2026); UNESCO Tentative List entry (Chile, 2004)
perspectives.account: Monte Verde II is a securely dated camp of about 14,500–14,800 cal BP, and scattered horizons at the nearby MV-I and Chinchihuapi localities may reach about 18,500 cal BP.

perspectives.holder: Surovell, Méndez, García, Lüthgens, Thompson and Latorre (Science, March 2026)
perspectives.account: Alluvial dates and an approximately 11,000-year-old tephra beneath the archaeological layer mean Monte Verde can be no older than the Middle Holocene, about 8,200–4,200 years BP, so it no longer anchors an early arrival in South America.

perspectives.holder: Waters, Halligan, Mandel, Holcomb, Davis and Holliday (Science eLetter, May 2026); Fundación Monte Verde
perspectives.account: Waters and colleagues argue the 2026 study mis-correlated its terrace deposits with the site stratigraphy, that its tephra may not be the Lepué Tephra, and that its own OSL ages show the creek surface existed by about 18,000–14,300 years ago. The foundation adds that the authors spent only hours on site and relied on non-archaeological deposits; both hold that the ~14,500-year age stands.

perspectives.holder: Indigenous voices reported by CBC News (2018): Willard Martin (Nisga'a elder), Oscar Dennis (Tahltan language conservationist), Woodrow Morrison (Haida elder), Paulette Steeves (Cree-Métis archaeologist)
perspectives.account: Martin said the Bering Strait account conflicts with Nisga'a oral history and origin stories; Dennis accepts a migration from Asia but by watercraft and reads origin stories as records of it; Morrison sees movement in several directions; Steeves argues the evidence for a single founding population is limited and that a Bering-only story is a colonial framing.
